issues.legal_issue: A pleading may be amended to add relief concerning disputed transfers when the existing pleading already contains the necessary factual basis, the amendment does not change the basic nature of the suit, and allowing it causes no prejudice or avoidable further litigation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs had brought a civil suit seeking an injunction against being forcibly dispossessed from land.
The defendants asserted in their written statement that they had acquired interests in the land through sale deeds.
The original plaint already set out the factual basis for challenging the transferors’ authority to sell and disputing the sale deeds’ effect on the plaintiffs’ rights.
The amendment sought relief concerning the validity of the sale deeds and a declaration of title, matters already in dispute between the parties.
The proposed relief was not barred in law when the amendment application was filed and could otherwise have been sought in a separate suit.
Allowing the amendment would not prejudice the defendants, who could file an additional written statement, and would avoid multiplicity of litigation.
The amendment was also prompted by an earlier observation that interim injunctive relief without seeking cancellation of the sale deeds was not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The amendment application should be allowed; the orders refusing it were set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy. The power is wide and is generally exercised liberally in the interests of justice, provided the amendment does not cause injustice or prejudice or change the basic nature of the suit. Where an application is made after trial has commenced, the proviso requires the court to be satisfied that, despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. The court reiterated the principles in J. Samuel and Others v. Gattu Mahesh and Others, (2012) 2 SCC 300, and Rameshkumar Agarwal v. Rajmala Exports Pvt. Ltd. and Others, (2012) 5 SCC 337. It relied on Pankaja v. Yellapa (Dead) by LRs. and Others, AIR 2004 SC 4102, (2004) 6 SCC 415, for the principles that an amendment serving justice and avoiding further litigation should be allowed and that a title-related relief does not introduce a different relief when its factual basis is already pleaded.

rule.if: civil_suit_pleading_amendment and necessary_factual_basis_already_pleaded and proposed_relief_addresses_existing_dispute and not basic_nature_changed and not relief_barred and not opposing_party_prejudiced and further_litigation_avoided

predicates.civil_suit_pleading_amendment: A party in a civil suit applied to amend its pleading.
predicates.necessary_factual_basis_already_pleaded: The original pleading already stated the material facts supporting the proposed relief.
predicates.proposed_relief_addresses_existing_dispu: The proposed relief concerns a matter already placed in dispute by the parties’ pleadings.
predicates.basic_nature_changed: The proposed amendment changes the basic nature of the suit.
predicates.relief_barred: The proposed relief was barred in law when the amendment was sought.
predicates.opposing_party_prejudiced: Allowing the amendment would cause prejudice to the opposing party that could not be addressed through a fair opportunity to respond.
predicates.further_litigation_avoided: Allowing the amendment would avoid the need for further litigation over the same dispute.
predicates.pleading_amendment_allowed: The court allows the pleading to be amended.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to amend a pleading in a civil suit, the amendment is allowed if its factual basis is already pleaded, it addresses an existing dispute without changing the suit’s basic nature, it is not barred or prejudicial, and it avoids further litigation.
